extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate or beginning graduate mathematics students studying metric spaces and elementary topology
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, propositions, and examples giving the basic structure and properties of (pseudo)metric and (pseudo)inner-product spaces: inequalities, topology (open/closed sets, interior, closure), continuity, sequences, subspaces, product spaces, and separation properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schwarz inequality (Lemma 2.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a pseudo inner-product space V with form (x,y) and pseudonorm k·k, for all x,y in V we have |(x,y)| ≤ kxk·kyk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof treats two cases (ky = 0 and ky ≠ 0), uses varying scalars and estimates; lemma is the analogue of the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality in the pseudo inner-product setting and was used earlier (Lemma 1.62) to obtain extra information in a special example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pseudonorm triangle inequality and metric construction (Proposition 2.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: If V is a pseudo inner-product space with form (·,·) and pseudonorm k·k, then k·k satisfies the norm-like properties (nonnegativity, homogeneity) and the triangle inequality kx + yk ≤ kxk + kyk; moreover d(x,y) := kkx − ykk defines a pseudometric on V (and a metric if the form is definite).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof computes kx + yk^2 = (x + y, x + y) and derives the triangle inequality via 2Re(x,y) ≤ 2| (x,y) | ≤ 2 kxk·kyk; shows pseudometric properties and notes definiteness yields metric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example: inner product from double integrals on power series (Example 14)
rubrics_metrics.description: On the complex vector space of power series with infinite radius of convergence, the integral ∬_D F(z) over the unit disk defines an inner product (F,G) = ∬_D F(z)overline{G(z)} dx dy and hence a metric d(F,G) = ||F − G||.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sketch of constructing inner-product spaces from integrals; used as an example that the proposition makes such V into a metric space with explicit metric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intersection of open balls is open (Lemma 2.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: If z lies in the intersection of two open balls B(r; x) and B(s; y) in a pseudometric space, then there exists t > 0 such that the open ball B(t; z) is contained in the intersection; consequently the intersection of two open balls is open.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct t = min{ r − d(x,z), s − d(y,z) } and use the triangle inequality to show B(t; z) ⊆ B(r; x) ∩ B(s; y). A figure is referenced for intuition in R^2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic properties of open sets (Proposition 2.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: The family of open sets in a metric space X satisfies: (a) X and ∅ are open, (b) arbitrary unions of open sets are open, (c) finite intersections of open sets are open.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses that open sets are unions of open balls and Lemma 2.4 to handle finite intersections. Remarks that these axioms will be taken as the axiomatic definition of topology later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interior equals largest open set contained in A (Proposition 2.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: The interior A^o of a subset A of X is the union of all open sets contained in A; equivalently it is the largest open set contained in A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: any open subset of A is a neighborhood for its points, so contained in A^o; conversely any x in A^o has an open neighborhood U contained in A, so x is in the union.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for openness via interior (Corollary 2.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: A subset A of X is open if and only if A = A^o (i.e., A equals its interior).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate from definition of interior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic properties of closed sets (Proposition 2.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: The closed sets of X satisfy: (a) X and ∅ are closed, (b) arbitrary intersections of closed sets are closed, (c) finite unions of closed sets are closed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follows by taking complements of the corresponding open-set statements (Proposition 2.5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit point and closure definitions and characterization (Proposition 2.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: A point x is a limit point of A if each neighborhood of x contains a point of A distinct from x. The closure A_cl of A is A together with all its limit points. A subset A is closed iff it contains all its limit points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses complements and neighborhoods: if Ac is open then points of Ac have neighborhoods disjoint from A, so cannot be limit points; conversely, if A contains all limit points then Ac is open.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closure equal intersection of closed sets containing A (Proposition 2.10)
rubrics_metrics.description: The closure A_cl of A is closed, and equals the intersection of all closed sets containing A; i.e., it is the smallest closed set containing A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: show A_cl contains all its limit points, hence closed, and any closed F ⊇ A must contain all limit points of A so contains A_cl.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idempotence of closure (Corollary 2.11)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any subset A, the closure of the closure equals the closure: (A_cl)_cl = A_cl.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follows from Proposition 2.10 and the fact that A_cl is already closed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotienting a pseudometric to a metric (Proposition 2.12)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a pseudometric space (X,d), define x ~ y iff d(x,y) = 0. The set X' of equivalence classes [x] carries a well-defined metric d'( [x],[y] ) := d(x,y), and (X',d') is a metric space. A subset A of X is open iff it is a union of equivalence classes and its image A' in X' is open.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof verifies reflexivity, symmetry, transitivity and that d' is well-defined; shows openness conditions via open balls and intersections with classes; this reduces pseudometric problems to metric ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epsilon–delta definition of continuity and neighborhood formulation
rubrics_metrics.description: A function f : (X,d) → (Y,ρ) is continuous at x ∈ X if for each ε>0 there exists δ>0 such that ρ(f(x), f(y)) < ε whenever d(x,y)<δ. Equivalently, for every neighborhood V of f(x) there is a neighborhood U of x with f(U) ⊆ V (Proposition 2.13).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposition 2.13 proves equivalence of the ε-δ and neighborhood formulations; emphasizes consistency with real-line continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of continuous functions is continuous (Corollary 2.14)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f : X → Y is continuous at x and g : Y → Z is continuous at f(x), then g ∘ f is continuous at x.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof applies Proposition 2.13 to first get neighborhood mapped inside and then compose neighborhoods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalences for continuity (Proposition 2.15)
rubrics_metrics.description: For f : X → Y between metric spaces the following are equivalent: (a) f is continuous at every point of X; (b) inverse image under f of every open set in Y is open in X; (c) inverse image under f of every closed set in Y is closed in X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard topological characterization of continuity; proof shows (a)⇔(b) via local neighborhoods and (b)⇔(c) via complements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distance from a point to a set is continuous (Definition & Proposition 2.16)
rubrics_metrics.description: For nonempty A ⊆ X define D(x,A) := inf{ d(x,y) : y ∈ A }. Then x ↦ D(x,A) is a continuous real-valued function on X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses triangle inequality: |D(x,A) − D(y,A)| ≤ d(x,y). Useful for constructing continuous functions separating sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity of x ↦ d(x,y) and closed balls (Corollaries 2.17 and 2.18)
rubrics_metrics.description: For fixed y, the function x ↦ d(x,y) is continuous. Consequently, closed balls { z : d(x,z) ≤ r } are closed sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corollaries follow from Proposition 2.16 (special case A = {y}) and Proposition 2.15(c) (preimage of closed interval). Remark: closed ball need not equal closure of open ball in all metrics (counterexample: discrete metric).

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of closure via distance (Proposition 2.19)
rubrics_metrics.description: For nonempty A ⊆ X, the closure A_cl equals { x ∈ X : D(x,A) = 0 }.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: set {x : D(x,A)=0} is closed and contains A, so contains A_cl; conversely if x ∉ A_cl there is r>0 with B(r;x) disjoint from A giving D(x,A) ≥ r > 0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness of limits in metric spaces (Proposition 2.20)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a metric space no sequence can converge to more than one point (limits are unique).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses separation of two distinct limit points by a positive distance and the triangle inequality to obtain contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of convergence in standard metric spaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Convergence in R, R^n (coordinatewise), C^n, extended real line R*, uniform convergence in B(S) (bounded functions) and bounded metric-valued functions; discrete metric sequences are eventually constant; indiscrete/pseudometric examples may have nonunique limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remarks compare different metrics on R^n (Euclidean vs max metric) and discuss uniform convergence and consequences like uniform boundedness of uniformly convergent sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous (Proposition 2.21)
rubrics_metrics.description: If fn : S → R (or metric space R) are bounded functions that converge uniformly to f and each fn is continuous at x0, then f is continuous at x0. In particular, uniform limits of continuous functions are continuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses triangle inequality and choosing N for uniform convergence, then δ for continuity of a given fn to control the three terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequences realize limit points and image characterization (Proposition 2.22)
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) If x is a limit point of A ⊆ X, there exists a sequence in A converging to x. (b) Any convergent sequence with limit x either has infinite image with x a limit point of its image or is eventually constant equal to x.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part (a): pick xn ∈ A ∩ B(1/n;x), xn ≠ x. Part (b): discard terms equal to x to get subsequence; if image finite then some value repeats infinitely often leading to eventual constancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closed set characterization by sequences (Corollary 2.23)
rubrics_metrics.description: A subset F of X is closed iff every convergent sequence in F has its limit in F.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follows from Proposition 2.22: sequences in F with limit give either limit point in F or eventually constant value in F.

rubrics_metrics.name: C(S) is closed in B(S) (Corollary 2.24)
rubrics_metrics.description: If S is a metric space, the set C(S) of bounded continuous scalar-valued functions on S is a closed subset of the metric space B(S) of bounded scalar-valued functions (with uniform metric).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses Proposition 2.21: uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous, combined with sequence characterization of closed sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequential criterion for continuity (Proposition 2.25)
rubrics_metrics.description: A function f : X → Y is continuous at x ∈ X iff for every sequence (xn) in X with xn → x, the sequence f(xn) converges to f(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: continuity gives neighborhood mapping of tail of sequence; conversely if preimages of all neighborhoods failed to contain any neighborhood then one could construct a sequence contradicting sequential continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subspace open/closed set characterization (Proposition 2.26)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is a subspace of (X,d), the open sets of A are exactly sets of the form U ∩ A with U open in X; the closed sets of A are exactly F ∩ A with F closed in X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open balls in A are intersections of open balls in X with A; closed sets follow by complements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction of continuous functions to subspaces (Corollary 2.27)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f : X → Y is continuous at a ∈ A and A ⊆ X is a subspace, then the restriction f|_A : A → Y is continuous at a. Conversely, continuity of f|_A can be checked using the image f(X) as range.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: neighborhoods in A arise as U ∩ A for U open in X; continuity on X yields such U mapping into neighborhood in Y.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product metrics and equivalence of product topologies
rubrics_metrics.description: On X × Y three natural metrics ρ1, ρ2, ρ_∞ (defined via sums, Euclidean, or max of d and d') all generate the same open sets and convergent sequences; convergence in product is equivalent to coordinatewise convergence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inequalities between ρ1, ρ2, and ρ_∞ show mutual neighborhood inclusion of balls and hence same topology; in R^n this recovers usual Euclidean topology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity of algebraic and elementary operations (Proposition 2.28 and Corollary 2.29)
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard operations are continuous: addition/subtraction and scalar multiplication in R^n and C^n, coordinate maps, absolute value, max/min, multiplication/division (where defined); products, sums, scalar multiples, and conjugation preserve continuity; reciprocals are continuous on nonzero domain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs reduce operations to compositions of previously established continuous maps and use product-space continuity and Proposition 2.25/Corollary 2.14. Remarks note that C(S) becomes a vector space and a vector subspace of B(S).

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity of the metric function d : X × X → R
rubrics_metrics.description: The distance function (x,y) ↦ d(x,y) is continuous on X × X (with product metric).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shown by appropriate inequalities: |d(x,y) − d(x0,y0)| ≤ max{d(x,x0), d(y,y0)}·2, giving explicit δ for given ε.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation properties of metric spaces (Proposition 2.30)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every metric space is T1 (singletons closed). For distinct points x,y there are disjoint open neighborhoods (Hausdorff). Metric spaces are regular and normal: given point and closed set or two disjoint closed sets, there exist disjoint open sets separating them; moreover one can find a continuous function f : X → [0,1] taking values 0 exactly on one closed set and 1 exactly on the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs use distance-to-set functions D(x,A) to build separating neighborhoods and continuous functions; Proposition 2.16 and 2.19 are instrumental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of a base for a metric space (Proposition 2.31)
rubrics_metrics.description: A family B of subsets of X is a base for the metric space iff (a) every member of B is open and (b) for every x ∈ X and open neighborhood U of x there is some B ∈ B with x ∈ B ⊆ U.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows equivalence with the usual topological definition of a base; open balls provide an example of a base in a metric space.
